newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Pacific Economic Cooperation Council upbeat on HK.
newsitem.headline: Pacific Economic Cooperation Council upbeat on HK.

text.p: Hong Kong remains on track for healthy growth and moderate inflation in 1997 and 1998, the Pacific Economic Cooperation Council (PECC) said on Tuesday.

"On the eve of the transfer of sovereignty, the Hong Kong economy is close to what seems to be a five percent trend rate of growth," the PECC said in a report. Economic growth should be close to five percent in both 1997 and 1998, it said.
The PECC said that strength in Hong Kong's asset market reflects optimism about the state of the economy after it becomes a Special Administrative Region of China.

"This optimism is generally well warranted, given China's steadfast reforms that are transforming it into a liberalized market economy," the PECC said. As China becomes more attractive to foreign investors, Hong Kong will benefit, the agency said.
With Hong Kong's trading partners either remaining strong or in a phase of continual recovery, Hong Kong's economic outlook for 1997 is quite favorable, the report said.
But the PECC cautioned that a stronger dollar could hurt Hong Kong's competitiveness. The Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the U.S. unit.
The PECC said that a stronger dollar is particularly worrying because business cost inflation in Hong Kong, particularly office and residential rental inflation, shows clear signs of rising again.
The PECC said it expects Hong Kong's retail sales to continue to improve noticeably in 1997, helped by improved confidence and a surge in tourism.
Investment activity is expected to remain healthy, led by infrastructure projects. Building activity is accelerating, largely in response to a perceived shortage of residental flats.
The PECC said it remains relatively optimistic about Hong Kong's inflation outlook, despite worrying cost inflation.
"There is a good chance that inflation will fall slightly, mainly on account of continuing weakness in wages and relatively modest rental increase," it said.
However, the PECC warned that it is imperative for Hong Kong to contain inflation and government spending if it wants to compete effectively in increasingly competitive world markets.

While the government is committed to keeping public expenditure growth in line with economic growth, it would be difficult for Hong Kong to roll back the entitlements, notably social security and transfers to the elderly, that have become an increasing proportion of government spending over the years.
"As a result, there are pressures to curtail or privatise public services," the PECC said.
If government spending creeps up -- and given its commitment to maintaining a low tax regime under the Basic Law -- the government will be under pressure to raise user charges.

"Fortunately, the government can count on a new source of revenue, namely land rent, that is collectible from most properties in the New Territories annually after the change in sovereignty," the PECC said.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
